opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think science is interesting precisely because it's a domain where we already know human intuition runs out. When you look at protein folding, materials, or the dynamics of a cell, you're dealing with spaces that are enormously high-dimensional, with interactions we can't hold in our heads. For a long time our way of coping was to simplify: we build a theory that a human can write on a blackboard, and we accept that it only captures part of the picture. A model doesn't have that constraint. It can learn patterns that don't compress nicely into a human-readable equation and still be predictive and useful.

The other thing I like about science as a test ground is that it has a built-in reality check. With language or images, it's very easy to be impressed by something that just sounds or looks plausible. In science, you can go to the lab and test it. Either the molecule binds or it doesn't. Either the material has the property you predicted or it doesn't. That gives you a way to tell whether a model is actually going beyond what we know, or just remixing what's already in its training data.

I'll add a note of caution, though, and it's something I've been thinking about a lot. Many of today's models are extremely good at interpolating within existing knowledge. They're like the perfect straight-A student who has read every paper. But the big scientific breakthroughs often came from someone asking a question nobody thought was worth asking, or challenging an assumption everyone shared. So for me the real question isn't only whether AI can solve problems faster than humans, but whether we can build systems that propose new questions and push against the consensus. Science is where we'll find out, because it's where the difference between knowing a lot and discovering something new is clearest.

r001.rationale: The response says models can learn patterns in high-dimensional scientific domains beyond human intuition, but it does not identify access to sensory modalities unavailable to humans as the reason.

fable-5.1.text:
Science is interesting because it's the one place where we actually have a clear sense of where human thinking runs out. In most domains, when you ask whether a model is "superhuman," the question is a bit fuzzy. Superhuman at writing an email? What would that even mean? But in science, the frontier is explicit. We know what we don't know. We know the questions we've been stuck on for decades, and we know roughly why we're stuck.

And a lot of the reasons we're stuck are very human reasons. One is the sheer volume. Nobody can read the whole literature anymore, even in a narrow subfield. So connections between, say, a materials science result and a biology result just never get made, not because they're hard to see but because no single brain ever holds both at once. A model can hold both. That's not intelligence in some deep sense, it's just not having our memory limits.

The second thing is more interesting to me, which is the way we think. Scientists are trained in a tradition. You learn a set of tools, a set of intuitions, from your advisor, who learned them from their advisor. That's wonderful, it's how knowledge compounds, but it also means we all explore the same corner of the space. The famous example is Einstein and relativity, where the problem is that you need to let go of an intuition everyone shares, in that case about time being absolute. Very few humans can do that. A model doesn't necessarily have that intuition baked in the same way, or at least you can imagine training it so that it doesn't.

So when I say "beyond human limitations," I don't mean the model is smarter in some mystical way. I mean there are specific, nameable constraints on how we do science, memory, attention span, disciplinary silos, inherited intuition, and science happens to be a domain where you can actually test whether removing those constraints produces something new. If a model proposes a hypothesis, you can go to the lab and check. That's rare. In most other domains we'd just be arguing about whether the output is good.

The thing I'd caution against is thinking this is already here. Today the models are very good at the first part, the reading and connecting, and honestly quite bad at the second part, at having a genuinely new idea rather than a plausible recombination of existing ones. Most of what you get is a sort of very well-read graduate student. But that's exactly why it's a good place to think. The gap between where we are and where we'd want to be is concrete, and you can measure progress against it rather than against vibes.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes models’ ability to retain and connect more literature and to avoid inherited human intuitions. It does not identify access to sensory modalities unavailable to humans as an existing route to superhuman scientific capability.

astra-6.text:
I think science is interesting because it gives you a way to evaluate a model beyond whether its answer sounds good to a human. You can ask: does this prediction agree with an experiment? Does this material actually have the properties we predicted? Reality becomes the judge.

With language, we often train models to imitate us, and then we ask humans to judge their outputs. That’s useful, but it can also put a ceiling on what we’re looking for. If a model comes up with something we don’t understand, we might simply rate it badly.

In science, an idea can be unfamiliar—even counterintuitive—and still be demonstrably correct. So you have room for a model to discover patterns or propose explanations that we wouldn’t have found ourselves. That doesn’t necessarily mean it’s a better scientist in every sense. But it gives us a concrete way to explore capabilities beyond our own intuition, while still checking that they work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating predictions against experiments and finding patterns beyond human intuition, but it does not identify access to sensory modalities unavailable to humans as a way scientific AI models can already be superhuman.

sol-6.1.text:
Science is interesting because we have a way to evaluate an answer that goes beyond whether it sounds right to a human. You can make a prediction and test it against the world. That gives AI a chance to discover something we don’t already understand, rather than just reproduce what we would say.

And human intelligence has limitations. We have intuitions about certain scales, certain kinds of objects, because those were useful to us. There’s no reason those intuitions should be the best ones for understanding molecules or very high-dimensional systems. A model might find patterns that are difficult for us to see.

The exciting question is whether it can lead us to a new hypothesis, a new experiment, something that expands our understanding. In science, being surprising can be valuable—but you still have to show that the prediction works.

r001.rationale: The response says models may find patterns humans struggle to see, but it does not identify access to sensory modalities unavailable to humans as a way they can already be superhuman.
